candidates.title: Titaner’s new torch lighter features a 4.5-billion-year-old meteorite outer shell
candidates.full_text:
In 1906, a few kids in northern Sweden were kicking rocks around for fun when they hit one that refused to budge. That stubborn lump turned out to be a piece of the Muonionalusta meteorite, a slab of space iron that landed near the Arctic Circle roughly a million years ago. More than a century later, Titaner is turning pieces of Muonionalusta into lighters. The Monolith’s Genuine Meteorite Edition pairs the meteorite with precision-machined titanium, and the whole lineup is designed for everyday carry. Honestly, I can think of worse retirement plans for a space rock than lighting someone’s cigar.

Titaner has spent about two decades machining titanium into pens, pry bars, knives, and even frying pans, so a titanium lighter sits squarely in its comfort zone. The meteorite changes the personality of the object. Every Meteorite Edition carries its own crosshatched slice of asteroid core and its own serial number, while every Monolith gets an ignition wheel and magnetic slider. There’s a removable copper heat sink, a replaceable insert, and a symbol for fire built into the side vents.

Click Here to Buy Now: $159 $286 (44% off). Hurry, only 77/100 left!

Muonionalusta’s crosshatch of intersecting bands is called a Widmanstätten pattern. It forms as nickel-iron alloys develop distinct crystal structures during the slow cooling of an asteroid’s core over millions of years. Muonionalusta itself is estimated to be over 4.5 billion years old, roughly the age of the solar system. Titaner’s tagline for the Monolith is “A star you can hold.” Asteroid core doesn’t have quite the same ring to it.

Titaner can’t control where those lines fall, which is sort of the point. The pattern on each Meteorite Edition Monolith depends on where and how the meteorite was cut, so each gets a different layout. One might show long diagonal streaks while another gets a tighter grid of intersecting bands. Each one also comes with an exclusive serial number and, according to Titaner, an independent material-testing certificate. The space-rock story comes with paperwork.

I don’t smoke, and I still want this lighter in my pocket. Titaner gave the Monolith two separate controls: an ignition wheel you roll with your thumb and a magnetic slider at the base. Up close, the optional hammered-texture wheel kit has faceted, CNC-machined knurling on its outer rings and a crosshatched grip in the center, intended to give your thumb more purchase with every roll. The mechanism looks like something you’d happily operate even with nothing to light.

The titanium components are precision-machined, with attention to the edges and surfaces your fingers meet. The metal brings strength, low weight, and corrosion resistance to an object destined to live in pockets and bags. Titanium is a poor conductor of heat, though, so Titaner adds a removable copper heat sink intended to help dissipate heat during use. The Cricket Flint Deluxe insert at its core is refillable with butane, so you top it up instead of tossing it. The insert is replaceable too, and the copper heat sink carries over to a compatible replacement.

The magnetic slider at the base moves between detents and looks dangerously easy to fidget with. Slide it to the refill position and it exposes the filling valve, so you can top up the butane without pulling the insert out. Tucked inside the slider is a spare flint, ready for when the original wears down. Remove the module entirely and its end doubles as a flathead tool for adjusting the insert’s gas flow. Swapping the insert itself means undoing a single M2 retaining screw at the bottom.

Up top, the Cricket Flint Deluxe platform produces what Titaner describes as a wind-resistant torch flame. Titaner built its own outer shell and heat-management components around that insert. A gap between the combustion chamber and the titanium shell connects to ventilation channels on the side, providing a path for airflow. That airflow is intended to work alongside the copper heat sink to dissipate heat during use.

Along the side of the Monolith, those ventilation slots are arranged to echo Li (☲), the fire trigram in the I Ching, the ancient Chinese book of divination. Li is associated with fire, light, and clarity, and Titaner pairs it with a sweet little blessing: “May your path be bright, and every step be clear.” It’s a fitting symbol to cut into a lighter and gives the body a recognizable signature. candidates.title: 7 Knife and EDC Picks That Run From Keychain to Premium Steel
candidates.full_text:
Tuesday’s carry desk ran wide, from a $260 premium folder with a ZDP-189 blade down to a keychain knife that costs less than a sandwich near the office. Six of these seven picks ran on Gadgeteer today, and each section links the full piece.

One fresh Spyderco deal joins the set, priced between the folders it shrinks from, and it hasn’t had a Gadgeteer piece of its own yet. The spread runs $20.99 to $260, and the only discount on the page sits on a CIVIVI flipper. Every price below was checked on Amazon this afternoon.

Spending more doesn’t always buy a longer blade, and the Ultra Pocket makes that case in ironwood. Its 3-inch ZDP-189 blade rides in a polished frame at 99 grams, sized to share a pocket with a phone and a wallet without crowding either one. Polished steel and compact dimensions carry the design, and the ironwood gives each handle its own grain, so no two of these look quite alike coming out of the box.

North Mountain Blade Ultra Pocket, desert ironwood 3-inch ZDP-189 blade · Desert ironwood handle · 6.73 inches overall · 99 g · Pocket clip Price: $260 Where to buy: Buy on Amazon

North Mountain sells a bigger sibling, the Lucky Dog, with a 4-inch SLD-Magic blade and its Kick Stop opener at $150. Reach costs less here. Buyers who want reach land on the Lucky Dog and keep $110.

One flipper design at four budgets is the Praxis family pitch, and the full-size C803F anchors the line at $42.50. A 3.75-inch 9Cr18MoV drop point opens on a flipper tab and locks with a liner lock, and the OD Green G10 handle stretches 8.43 inches overall at 4.42 ounces.

CIVIVI Praxis C803F, OD Green G10 3.75-inch 9Cr18MoV drop point · Flipper opening Price: $42.50 $50.00 (save $7.50, 15% off) Where to buy: Buy on Amazon

Gift buyers get a clean ladder here. A first knife from this family teaches the same grip and opening motion at every size.

Short version: the C803F is the work pick of the four.

Spyderco’s Tenacious formula shrinks in the Persistence Lightweight, a 2.77-inch blade with the same steel, lock and four-position clip carried over from the bigger knife. It disappears in a pocket. Amazon’s black oxide build at $56.25 is the cheapest way into the family this week.

Spyderco Persistence Lightweight, black oxide 2.77-inch 8Cr13MoV blade, full flat grind · FRN handle · Liner lock · Four-position pocket clip Price: $56.25 Where to buy: Buy on Amazon

It rides flat against the leg through a full workday, and the sub-3-inch blade stays legal in towns that cap carry length. Carriers who found the Tenacious one size too big get the same full flat grind and the same liner lock in a frame a pocket forgets about. The cut quality stays right where the value line built its name.

Prying with a pocketknife tip is how good blades get chipped. The Kursor Mini exists so the knife never takes that job. Kansept built it as a 3.49-inch titanium bar with a black G10 inlay, a blackwash finish and a pocket clip, designed by Justin Koch of Koch Tools. Dedicated leverage is the brief, and the bar shape puts a flat pry edge where a blade tip should never go.

Kansept Kursor Mini Pry Bar, blackwash titanium 3.49-inch titanium body · Black G10 inlay · Integrated pocket clip · Interchangeable scales · Koch Tools design, model G015C2 · Flat pry edge for paint cans, battery covers and stubborn lids Price: $52.58 Where to buy: Buy on Amazon

Scales swap for other colors and materials across the Kursor line, so the black build here is one configuration among several, with different finishes up and down the range. At $52.58 it costs less than replacing one snapped tip.

Orange does the talking on the RAT II . The carry hardware backs it up: a textured handle, a satin blade and a four-position clip make a practical everyday folder that rides on either side of the pocket. Amazon’s $45.25 also undercuts the $46.19 the Ontario roundup printed this morning. It’s the middle pick of the three Ontario knives covered today, priced between the keyring Traveler and the camp fixed blade.

Ontario RAT II, orange Satin blade · Textured orange handle · Four-position pocket clip · Liner lock · Model ON8860OR · One of three Ontario knives in today’s roundup piece, with the Traveler and the ADK High Peaks Price: $45.25 Where to buy: Buy on Amazon

candidates.title: A Floating Cultural Center Where the Library Refuses to Stay Put
candidates.full_text:
A broad roof, a wooden porch, and lights reflected in the water: El Embarcadero looks more like a neighborhood gathering spot than a grand cultural institution. That feels right. Designed by Natura Futura in Babahoyo, Ecuador, the completed floating cultural center addresses a basic absence. According to the architects, its Barreiro neighborhood lacks public educational, cultural, and social spaces. The river is where they’ve chosen to make room.

Water also complicates the brief. The architects say seasonal rises reduce local accessibility for roughly 25–30% of the year. El Embarcadero responds with a floating structure and mooring systems designed for fluctuating water levels, alongside amphitheater steps that can flood. I like that the design accepts changing conditions without treating the neighborhood’s relationship with the river as something to eliminate.

The building’s appearance supports that sense of belonging. Photographs show timber walls and a generous covered deck, with a broad roof projecting beyond the enclosed rooms. It has the visual familiarity of a porch, somewhere you might pause before deciding to go inside. For a cultural center, I’d take that approachable presence over an entrance designed primarily to make visitors feel small. The building looks connected to everyday life along the bank.

Its approximately 33-by-52-foot platform accommodates a library, community kitchen, educational spaces, offices, and shared areas. Blackboard-and-mirror panels and furniture that doubles as book storage allow the interior to change with different activities. Those choices make sense to me at this scale. A neighborhood building shouldn’t need a separate, permanently designated room for every possible use. The useful question is how much can happen within the space without making each activity feel like an awkward accommodation.

The library’s reach extends beyond that platform. A companion Library Canoe is designed to carry books and workshops to more distant riverfront homes and communities, using El Embarcadero as its base. It’s my favorite element because it changes the question of access. Providing a room full of books matters, but so does considering who can reach that room. Here, a familiar vessel becomes part of the cultural infrastructure, rather than something parked outside it.

That familiarity has a history. Project supporter rearc institute documents a local floating-house tradition sustained by fishing, boatbuilding, and river trade, as well as Natura Futura’s work with river residents since 2019. El Embarcadero belongs to the broader Huellas del Agua initiative, which includes neighborhood regeneration and floodable public landscapes. That context matters. I read the center as an extension of knowledge already present in Babahoyo, not an imported architectural idea looking for an interesting waterfront site.

The programming gives that interpretation some substance. Reporting on the opening, Ecuadorian newspaper EXTRA described a library collection of more than 400 volumes and plans for free weekly cultural activities. Cultural manager Lincoln Meza discussed making room for artists, writers, organizers, and residents with knowledge to share. That’s an appealing definition of a cultural center: somewhere local people can contribute to the program, rather than simply arrive to watch someone else perform.

Of course, a building’s opening doesn’t establish how well it will serve people over time. I’d want to know how consistently the workshops run, how the canoe service develops, and how the spaces work through changing river conditions. Those are fair questions for a project whose value depends on repeated use. The architecture provides a framework, but a full calendar and dependable stewardship will give that framework its purpose.

Still, El Embarcadero offers a persuasive idea of what a public building can look like when its starting point is the neighborhood around it. I’m drawn to the modesty of that ambition. There’s room for reading, cooking, teaching, and gathering, with a canoe intended to take some of those activities farther. The measure of success I’d care about is whether residents begin treating the center as an ordinary, dependable part of their week.
